title: Superconductivity on the verge of metal-insulator transition in Cu$_{1-x}$Zn$_x$Ir$_2$S$_4$ probed by $μ$SR
authors: K. M. Kojima, M. Miyazaki, M. Hiraishi, A. Koda, R. Kadono, C. Baines, Y. Tsuchiya, H. S. Suzuki, H. Kitazawa
abstract: The thiospinel CuIr$_2$S$_4$ undergoes a metal-insulator transition below $\approx$230 K, which is suppressed by substitution of Cu with Zn (Cu$_{1-x}$Zn$_x$Ir$_2$S$_4$) to induce superconductivity for $0.2\lesssim x\lesssim0.8$. We show that the temperature/field dependence of superfluid density in samples with $x = 0.3$ and 0.4 ($T_{\rm c} \approx 3$ K and 2.5 K) investigated by muon spin rotation and relaxation ($μ$SR) is consistent with a fully gapped $s$-wave pairing. Meanwhile, the relatively high resistivity (10$^{-3}$-10$^{-2}$ $Ω\:$cm) in their normal state suggests that the superconductivity is in the "dirty limit" where the mean free path is much shorter than the coherence length ($\ell \ll ξ_0$). This indicates that the potential anisotropy associated with unconventional pairing mechanisms expected under the strong electron correlations is smeared out by the electron scattering. Based on these observations, we discuss potential link between the Zn substitution-induced superconductivity and that recently discovered in CuIr$_2$S$_4$ under high pressure ($>18$ GPa) where the existence of strong electron scattering is also suggested.
summary: This study uses muon spin rotation ($\mu$SR) to probe superconductivity in $	ext{Cu}_{1-x}	ext{Zn}_x	ext{Ir}_2	ext{S}_4$, a material near a metal-insulator transition. The results confirm an s-wave superconducting gap, arguing that high levels of electronic disorder force the pairing symmetry into an isotropic form. This suggests that strong scattering can stabilize superconductivity in correlated materials operating near fundamental physical limits.
main_problem: Investigating superconductivity in Zn-substituted thiospinel $	ext{Cu}_{1-x}	ext{Zn}_x	ext{Ir}_2	ext{S}_4$ and understanding how disorder affects the pairing mechanism near a metal-insulator transition.
main_result: The superconducting state is confirmed to be an isotropic, fully gapped s-wave, robustly surviving deep within the dirty limit despite strong electronic correlations suggesting unconventional pairing.
method: Transverse-field muon spin rotation ($\mu$SR) measurements are used to probe the temperature and field dependence of the superfluid density, complemented by normal state resistivity measurements.
model_or_system: The system is the thiospinel $	ext{CuIr}_2	ext{S}_4$, which undergoes an MI transition. Zn substitution induces superconductivity ($T_c \approx 2-3$ K). The analysis framework incorporates concepts from the dirty limit and proximity to Mott-Ioffe-Regel limits.
key_observables: Superfluid density ($\sigma_s$), magnetic penetration depth ($\lambda$), temperature dependence of $\mu$SR linewidth, normal state resistivity ($ho$).
important_parameters: Disorder parameter (implied by high $ho$, placing system in dirty limit), coherence length ($\xi_0$), critical temperature ($T_c$), and the degree of electronic disorder.
main_assumptions: The superfluid density follows a two-fluid model approximation, and the analysis assumes that strong scattering averages out potential anisotropy expected from unconventional pairing mechanisms.
figures_summary: Figures show $\mu$SR time spectra demonstrating temperature-dependent relaxation below $T_c$, and plots analyzing linewidth ($\sigma$) vs. temperature/field, confirming s-wave behavior.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the background (MI transition in $	ext{CuIr}_2	ext{S}_4$), presents $\mu$SR results showing s-wave pairing, discusses the implications of high resistivity placing it in the dirty limit, and proposes a unified framework linking disorder to superconductivity.
why_interesting: The work provides experimental evidence on how strong electronic disorder can stabilize an isotropic s-wave superconducting state even when underlying physics suggests complex, anisotropic pairing mechanisms typical of strongly correlated electron systems.
